10973592.notes:
Comes with an A4-sized hardback book in Japanese with liner notes, a diary, many pictures and an interview with Yoko Ono.

[u]The liner notes by Kazumi Oguro (editor of Sotokoto magazine and president of Kirakusha which published this DVD+book set, also the owner of the Mpata Lodge mentioned in the text below) translate as follows[/u]:

[i]You can feel it all over you, Africa. The rising sun, the clouds dancing in the blue sky, the grass, the heat of the desert, the voice of the elephants. Let us drink from the water of Africa. That rhythm originated by humans, may it awaken us. The world is still young, humanity is still young. In search of wisdom, we continue to wander. Ryuichi Sakamoto, what did you see in Africa?[/i]

Nairobi[/b]
[i]Nairobi also has a Ground Zero. The American Embassy that was blown up in 1998 is situated there. It is now a park. The US embassy has moved to the suburbs and is now probably more secure. Many of the victims were Kenyans who were in a building next to the embassy that collapsed in the explosion. Perhaps the people in Japan don't remember much about this incident in a far distant world such as this. The people of Nairobi are said to have been deeply traumatized. That's right. Only after 9/11 would you realize that. It may be a human thing.[/i]

Museum[/b]
[i]The National Museum of Nairobi with its wide-ranging exhibits is quite spectacular. It has replicas of many ape and hominid specimens. And folk crafts of various tribes from all over Kenya. A taxidermy of a large number of birds. A tribe of scholars who have been excavating for generations, Louis, Richard and Meave of the Leaky family, have also managed this museum, in which Ryuichi Sakamoto seems to enjoy a moment of conversation with his ancestors. In front of the beautifully reproduced mural painting of the cave, you can see the cutting-edge information drawn by the ancient humans at that time. From ancient times onwards, humans have used animals as an expression. I want to meet them. I want guidance on how to reach them. I'm thinking urgently.[/i]

Nariokotome[/b]
[i]Hot. The air, it's hot. Passing through the heat wave, it's as if we're being boiled.
Lake Turkana, a beautiful blue lake also called "Jade Sea". Surrounding it, lava that spouted long ago before solidifying, a rocky mountain reminiscent of the early days of the earth, Acacia scattered around, and a breeze. This rugged and harsh nature spreads outwards. Anyway, it's hot out here. The observed temperature will exceed 40 degrees Celsius. Even if the wind blows, it's blowing hot air, but still it's better than nothing. The skin being burnt is unbearable except for the warm breeze. Any sweat dries up as soon as it appears. That's why our shirts are dry as well. If you notice, a large amount of water is lost from the body. If you forget to drink water, you won't make it in this world.
Such a scorching sun we're under. Ryuichi Sakamoto, however, walks around as if he doesn't care. This is the Great Rift Valley, the cradle of humankind. In it, the Lake Turkana area is known for its many fossil excavation sites.
I want to know the origin of people and get a glimpse of our ancestors. And to use it as food to think about what humanity is. That's also what Sakamoto has been thinking about since the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks. Why does humanity destroy things carefully, systematically, and using the great power of science? Will we repeat the follies that may kill humans, kill nature, and ruin the earth?
Perhaps the answer cannot be found by simply investigating the politics or the economics. That way you'll just be fooled and get lost. It can only be found in more fundamental places. And so we've come to this place. After all, he is a "professor" who's been curious from the start and wants to know about anything. Sakamoto is excited to talk to a man of legend, Kamoya Kimeu, in the land where humanity was born.
Kamoya Kimeu is from the Kamba tribe and has been involved in excavation work since he was young. He was on the main staff of the father and mother of East African archeology, paleoanthropology and biology, Louis and Mary Leakey. Kamoya also worked with his son's generation, i.e. Louis' son Richard and his wife Meave who inherited the research and excavation activities in the Leaky family. He's called the leader of the Hominid Gang, the Kenyans looking for fossils of human ancestors.
Born in 1940 when Kenya and Tanzania were part of the East Africa Protectorate, Kamoya grew up without any special education. He learned everything from Mr. and Mrs. Leakey. His soul must have been made specially for this. His dignity, intellect, and character all earned the respect of his colleagues, and the Leaky family trusted him more than anyone else. And Sakamoto is equally fascinated by his personality.
"It was around here, where I found it."
Says Kamoya. At a place where the hills have been destroyed by excavations, leaving some small hills and the flat land surrounding them. The small pieces that had casually risen up to the surface when the excavation had just gotten started. This was in 1984.
"You can tell by touching it, fossils have a different feel. I thought it might be some kind of fossil."
The piece was exactly that, of a Hominid. And a special one too. It was the first piece of an almost complete fossil of Homo erectus, the missing link between the monkeys and the newcomers. The fossil is presumed to belong to a 9-year-old boy, hence the name "boy". Turkana Boy, or Nariokotome Boy, from the place name of the discovery site.
The fact that several species of Hominids existed around the same time in the same region can no longer be denied from the research on Kenyanthropus platyops, which was later discovered by Meave Leakey. Even if human ancestors were competing for the same food and killing each other, it was a race to survive and will be found in other species. However, it's the terrible murdering by Homo sapiens that made them come out on top in that way.
Homo sapiens, with the largest and most complex brain. Homo sapiens, who destroy more lives than anyone else.
Nariokotome is on the west bank of Lake Turkana. Apparently it means "black elephant" to the Turkana tribe of nomads living around here. The area around Turkana looks barren now, but in the first half of the 20th century, white hunters came here to kill elephants. If so, the elephants must have been living around here from ancient times onwards and probably quietly watched the Homo erectus. Why did some of the Homo erectus people leave Nariokotome, Turkana, and Africa? And as time went on, Homo sapiens appeared, and what kind of interactions did they have with the Erectus people? That whole story and the mystery that human beings want to solve, the elephants must have been watching it.[/i]

El Molo[/b]
[i]This is exactly what it means when something takes your breath away. When visiting the village of El Molo, from the 4WD we first saw a flat land that looked like a thin layer of green at the end of the rocky shores of desolate Lake Turkana. You can see a hill and below it the lake that looks as beautiful as the name Jade Sea implies. Green and blue. When you climb the hill, below it you will see the open indentation and in that most beautiful of places, you can see the round houses made of doum palm leaves. It is just a picture. The legendary El Molo people live there. Nowadays it is forbidden to catch alligators, which is their specialty, and it is becoming more difficult year after year to protect their ethnic identity.[/i]

Turkana[/b]
[i]It takes about 2 hours to get to Turkana from Nairobi using a chartered Cessna plane. It lands on the airstrip at Loiyangalani on the southeastern tip. There is a shack at the airstrip, it says "VIP Lounge". A good joke. However, in the hot air at Turkana, the roof of the shack was well appreciated. Loiyangalani, which means where there is a tree, has doum palms and other flowerings, it is certainly an oasis. A place with the name Oasis Lodge welcomes Sakamoto. This lodge, which has been operating here for decades, has a great pool and a restaurant with a cozy bar where the German owners always drink a beer or vodka. Of course there are no windows in the restaurant, it is too windy. 
Next to this lodge there is a "Cultural Center", in which women from the surrounding tribes gather to make folk crafts and leather costumes in order to protect the traditional culture of each tribe. Of course, it has aspects of a consumer business, such as selling what they create and performing traditional dances, but basically the purpose is to protect their identity, which would disappear if simply left alone. The surrounding tribes are the Turkana and Masai peoples known to be militant nomads, the Samburu tribe known for their more decorative and splendid costumes, the Rendille tribe who keep camels and survive in the desert zone, and live on the waterfront. Then there are 4 El Molo tribes who used to hunt and eat crocodiles.
Originally, the tribes of Kenya each formed their own community, each basically living in their own world but, due to the poverty of each tribe and so-called modernisations like the development of the education system, some tribes have found it quite difficult to maintain their independence. Around Loiyangalani, the Samburu, Rendille and Turkana live quite adjacent to each other and as for the whole El Molo Bay area, it totally accepts people of other tribes in the villages. It seems that these people, who are said to be "phantom people" and are worried about extinction, are accepting the blood of other tribes to survive. The El Molo people lived on the shores of Lake Turkana, catching alligators and fish. They mixed with the Samburu when they were starving in the 18th century, and apparently Samburu became the main language used. It is also known that drinking the water of Lake Turkana, which is too alkaline, caused their skeletons to change, and many people became sick. In both the El Molo and Samburu villages, there are many children and young people who can even speak English. That's because the mission built a school, and they go there. Christianity is still striving to spread its teachings around the world. So, a child calling itself Jeremiah or Francis will call out to him as Good Morning.
Any children who "can" will go to junior high school, study more English at a boarding school and then come back to the village. Guiding around foreign visitors is an important source of income for the village. Ben and Macamba, who helped Ryuichi Sakamoto with his interviews, were also young people in this situation. Ben was a 24 year-old Samburu. Macamba was a 23 year-old Turkana. Both are strong, fashionable, attentive and smart. Macamba claimed there was a village of witch doctors in Turkana, so part of the shooting team went there. For 2 hours, the 4WD went on a road that was not a road, overcoming rolling stones and rocks. Then we got to a point where I could not drive any further, and we walked for 15 minutes. There, the Turkana culture of living was the way it had always been. The witch doctor had an eye full of wisdom and empathy. It took some time for Macamba to negotiate a guarantee for a shooting, to persuade him to be willing to let us take pictures of their daily lives. They were very interested in our camcorders and recorders. Especially with regards to their singing voices. The men of Turkana are poets. It is the men who create the songs. And the women started dancing to the songs.
At Loiyangalani, the mother of the Cultural Center gathered people to dance under a tree. Dance is about communication, and I was shown the basics. The soul and body are having fun colliding with each other, and laughter bursts out. A aura of light shimmers away, like when new life is born.
Ben wants to do more studying. He really wants to go to college. What religion do they believe in? He says he believes in the gods of each tribe. Perhaps their gods are primitive and childish according to Western scholarship. Just like what's being said about the eight million gods of Japan. El Molo's Jeremiah said with a sparkling eye that the only god was the Christian god. He is 10 years old and knows no vice.
When I asked for contact information at the time of our farewell, Macamba did not hesitate to teach me about the mission church. When Sakamoto asked, don't you believe in it? I answered and smiled, I'll use whatever I can, isn't that okay?

Everywhere humankind lived there exist mural paintings. Probably humans have always been very fond of drawing. African murals often depict animals and humans. The urge to record people's activities. Even for cultures that for a long time didn't have words, the mural paintings convey a lot of information. And when I look at the songs and dances of the Turkana people, I can't say for sure because there are no recorded materials, but I'm sure the prototypes of these songs and dances were enjoyed even in that era of murals. Music must have been a means of communication, an expression of the heart, and a joyful blessing.[/i]

Masai Mara[/b]
[i]An elementary school in Kenya is like a combination of elementary school and junior high school in Japan, and is attended by students up to the age of 14. With regards to the elementary school here in Masai Mara, the school building was a little old and it lacked facilities. Two years ago, Ryuichi Sakamoto, having come to Mpata Lodge, decided to help renovate the school building. Since then, I make a visit here every time I come. The children are always welcoming. But until now, they didn't know what this funny Japanese guy could do. This time, Sakamoto brought a piano. To donate. The children had never seen a piano. With cheers, the Masai children enjoyed their first piano with Sakamoto.[/i]

Mpata Lodge[/b]
[i]"Hey, you built a hotel like this in a place like this."
Ryuichi Sakamoto murmurs with a sigh. Having a cup of coffee at the restaurant at Mpata Lodge. 1 hour by regular Cessna flight from Nairobi, 30 minutes by Lodge-owned Land Rover from Kichwa Tembo Airstrip in Masai Mara National Reserve. On the hills of Oloololo overlooking the reserve, there are two lodges distributed in the shape of birds spreading their wings. The clubhouse in the center has a restaurant and bar, a swimming pool and a library. There is a Baboon bar outdoors.
Originally, it was a story of recklessness to build a lodge here. It's separate from the Masai Mara area, where you can see the most animals in Kenya. It's not in the reserve, but one person from Japan runs a hotel in a place overlooking it. Around 1984, this man who had such a dream was advised no one could do it. No, people just laughed and took it as a joke. However, he overcame many question marks and concluded negotiations with the local Masai landowner. It was constructed by acquiring members in a club format and in a foreign country, where it is a big task to secure transportation and infrastructure, and sometimes having to kick down in front of other big hurdles, he managed to arrive at the grand opening in 1993.
What impressed Sakamoto first of all is the splendor of the location. The terraces of all rooms overlook the reserve. Around the lodge, there are the Masai villages and water areas where giraffes and zebras gather. The lodge itself is quite large, so without going outside you can see various plants, birds, and Sakamoto's favourite, the beautifully coloured lizards. Baboons may even come to your terrace.
The suite-variety lodge is equipped with an outdoor jacuzzi, so you can enjoy the nature of Africa while feeling it on your skin. No, just slowly settling on the terrace and looking at the sky while listening to the sounds of animals and birds and the sound of the wind without entering the jacuzzi is also paradise.
"When I first came here, I could clearly see only a smaller area of that savanna. I had developed a bad eye in the city, without knowing it. Now I can see much more beyond."
Sakamoto is amazed this building is so solid and was done in such good taste. It was designed by Edward Suzuki. Being influenced by Buckminster Fuller, who emphasized coexisting with the environment, Suzuki was the perfect architect when the idea of establishing this lodge came up. When building the hotel in this place, the most important consideration was to coexist with the environment and to coexist with the Masai tribe. Spacious rooms, roofs that incorporate African flair. And Suzuki was particular about Den, the library. There are many books in the open space of Den, and there is also a desk for reading large items such as photography books. Use of daylight was also taken into account, which is perfect for spending the afternoon reading.
Of course, Masai Mara is full of fun activities such as a balloon safari to watch animals in the early morning from a balloon in the sky, a game drive to observe many animals nearby, a safari on foot to collect animal footprints with plaster, walking safely on the savanna with your own feet. But it's also fine to just visit and read a book. Even if you don't go to the safari, the sound, the wind, and the smell will make you fully experience Masai Mara.
I am also happy with the service with a nice smile by the Masai and other employees from multiple tribes. At dinner-time when a full-course French meal prepared by Chef Kiyomi Mikuni is served, the neighboring Masai may perform a dance. The welcome dance by the employees is also a fun entertainment. Dedicated naturalists and drivers entertain guests with pride in their chests. Sakamoto, a regular, is already being greeted with a smile and a welcome back.
"When I first heard about a hotel in Kenya, I thought I might never go that far, but that's ridiculous because I've been here for three years in a row."
Ryuichi Sakamoto's hideout in Kenya. Today at Mpata Lodge, a relaxing time has passed by.[/i]

Masai[/b]
[i]It is said the ancestors of the Masai first moved south along the Nile from northern Africa. It seems they settled at Lake Turkana in around the 15th century. According to their oral tradition, the first memory of the Masai is that they lived in a place like the inside of a crater. Surrounded as it was by cliffs, the outside world was completely invisible.
At some point, they ran out of water and food. Looking up, they saw birds nestling in green leaves above the cliffs. When out of the hardship the brave young man who noticed that ventured out, there existed fertile land. They all had a lot of trouble building something like a bridge to be able to go up and out, but it broke along the way, and a division in 2 occurred, those who fell down and those who did make it out. After that their language became completely different and they became a different tribe. Some of the remaining tribes made it out later, but they became Somali and live in a different world from the Masai.
If you know the nature around Turkana, you will feel the power of persuasion this legend has.
By the way, the Masai who went further south after "Deturkana" found the area called Masai Land where they mainly live now. The same is true around Nairobi, in the areas called Masai Mara and Serengeti. The weather is nice, it's a fertile and wonderful place for them and their cows. The Masai must be very proud to occupy such land.
On the other hand, the Masai drove out other tribes that lived there. They defeated strong tribes such as the Galla and the Oromo, whereas tribes like the Kikuyu and Chaga that did not resist much were driven into Mount Kenya and Mount Kilimanjaro, and even now, the Masai are indifferent compared to other nomads. They are strong. Of course, there are also Masai who are kind and who smile. But they're not kind because they're so-called "Masai for sightseeing". Also, just because he has a gentle face, does not mean he is always peaceful. When things become exciting, an aggressive side may show and he may turn into a wolf.
In all, the Masai seem to be making more demands in protecting their culture and way of life than other tribes. This may have something to do with "the pride of the tribes that were victors". For them, for example, the tribes of Samburu were the ones who couldn't reach their level, and the Turkana were madmen when they chose to live in such harsh nature and as a result they maybe think of them as losers. In Kenya, there is a term for tribes that don't have cows, and for poor people etc. and in the old days it was misunderstood as if it was the name of a tribe, but it is actually the Masai word for those who do not have cows or, in other words, it seems to refer to a deceased person who is not able to contribute.
After all, the Masai seriously believe that all cows all around the world are in their possession. Cows are a symbol of wealth and are irreplaceable to anyone. If you have a lot of cows, no matter how bad a man you are, you are a man of virtue. Those who have a lot of cows also have lots of wives.
There has been conflict among the Masai tribes. A number of clans (tribes) have been destroyed. Are they too warrior-like? For example, for them killing a human who is not Masai does not mean murder. Of course, in modern times they are judged by Kenyan law, not by tribal law. Having heard this, the Masai are not just violent persons, and they only attack white people when something terrible is done. The Masai god is in the Masai, and there is order.
They know about cows. By heart it is connected with the spirit of the forest. They are well aware what plants are good for which diseases or which are poisons that kill people. Apparently there are still conflicts within the tribe and with other tribes around them. I don't know if they understand terrorism, but I do know that they would have a reason for an attack. And the rules they follow when fighting are very strict.
"Don't drive the weak into the forest"
Apparently that's a saying among them. This means that if the opponent is in a vulnerable position, you shouldn't intimidate him any further.
"Don't ask for new scars"
This means revenge is evil.
The boys want to wear Masai cloth everywhere in the world. The power of the naughty Masai seems to stem from an innocent energy that is unsuitable for capitalist powers.[/i]

Elephant[/b]
[i]Something can be heard in the distance, it may be a distant thunder. But perhaps our ears heard the murmurs of grass-grazing animals tens of kilometers away. Even with low-frequency sounds that are said to be inaudible to humans, in the savanna our whole body and the earth and the air resonate, and we may be able to feel something. It even makes me feel like that. There are elephants in the savanna.

Elephants are animals with excellent communication skills. By making full use of sounds that humans cannot hear, they communicate various intentions to each other. They're able to distinguish the voices of 100 animals in a certain area, not only the voices of their kind but also those of humans. They can also smell them. They genuinely remember the person who did something it did not like. Face-to-face with elephants, humans cannot lie. Their true identity has been discovered by them. You better believe this.
If you are delicate and nervous, no matter how insensitive you are to it, they will feel any spicy vibrations in the air. And when you relax, an elegant atmosphere envelops their whole body.
The elephants have lived on this planet for so long that we humans and others have not been able to deal with them.
What did the elephants think when long ago our human ancestors came down from the trees and appeared in the savanna? These naughty little animals, did they laugh when they couldn't handle them? Did what would happen in the future come out with a deep rumble (a groan)? No, they probably spent their time relaxing while looking sideways, just like they do now.

Mankind has not listened to the words of elephants for a long time. To the contrary, they even tried to force them out. We hunted elephants with spears at one time, shot them with guns at other times, instilled fear at another time, and intimidated them at yet another time. In Asia, elephants were tamed and used as luggage carriers and as tanks. Of course, some do try to interact with elephants. Why is that? It appears many women are involved in this.
Joyce Poole is one of the women who listens to the words of elephants. She examines the lives of elephants in detail and records their voices. She listens to various sounds and examines their reactions. What is the composition of the elephant family and how do they live? How do male and female elephants love each other? Through the studies of Joyce, the ecology of elephants has gradually become understood, and they have dramatically increased the understanding of elephants.
In her laboratory overlooking the Great Rift Valley, the voices of elephants are analyzed, revealing the mystery of their life that humanity did not know about.
A herd of elephants is a female-led family. A benevolent female elephant boss draws the herd. They decide things through discussions and avoid mischievous attacks. The motherhood governs the offspring.
At a certain age, the males leave the offspring and enter a loose group of only females. Is it not possible to maintain the herd when a male is in heat, "musth" this phase is called, which can lead to a time when it loses itself and become violent? Is it the wisdom of elephants cultivated over many years to keep the family intact? Some herds may also live in groups in order to protect each other.

Can you hear the voices of the elephants? If you listen, you can hear them in the savanna, in the crowds in Nairobi, in the desert of Turkana, and so on. Can't you see the illusion of a walking elephant in some distant memory?
There must have been a lot of discussion among the elephants, while humans were killing each other, or while humans were killing elephants and buying and selling their ivory. Even while believing that humans are tame elephants and some kind of acrobats, the elephants must have communicated several experiences to each other and deepened each other's knowledge.
Elephants talking, elephants resonating, their voices overlapping to call for a new vibration. To create a network of that sound on earth.
Homo sapiens is said to be the primate of all things. What is a primate? It's an embodiment of stubbornness, believing that we are excellent, with masses of arrogance, believing that we are right. It's the animals who live in harmony with the environment without using any tools to communicate with each other in the harsh nature and to protect each other. When faced with this ability to communicate with their kind and with voices far away, what does it mean to be proud of the Internet?
The earth has lived quietly with the elephants. They may have evolved slowly. Slowly enough that it seems like nothing has changed in our time.
Without becoming impatient, we too should want to enjoy the conversations with them. And perhaps someday in the distant future we can reach that state of true maturity.[/i]

NY[/b]
[i]Sunset in New York falls early. Our retinas still set on the African horizon, our biological clocks still moving in African time. In this dangerous place, I'm about to miss that.
People from all over the world are spending their time here. Out of Africa, mankind wandered to skyscraper towns such as this. Incredible destruction is also the result of incredible construction.
Borders are empty, the walls between people are empty. With a little imagination, you should know there is essentially no separation between the Turkana people, the Masai people, and the United States people.
All people laugh when they're enjoying themselves. All people sing, dance, eat and sleep. The sounds ring out, the melodies flow, and the rhythms ripple.
I notice that Africa is everywhere. Life is everywhere. How about God? Where is God and what is he doing? The shadow of an elephant is also noticeable on Manhattan Island. I hear the echo of an elephant. A car passes through while whispering the question of what kind of animal humans are. We continue our journey immature and underdeveloped, on an endless quest full of uncertainties.[/i]

[u]The diary that was kept by Ryuichi Sakamoto translates as follows[/u]:

2002.02.05 Tuesday
@Nairobi[/b]

[i]Nairobi. The first day of shooting. At 8:30, I leave the hotel and go to the former site of the American Embassy, which is now a park. I am surprised at the small size of the site. The names of the victims engraved on the stone monument are all locals. There seems to be a separate monument for the victims that belonged to the embassy staff. Why this separation? Didn't the people in Nairobi suffer the same trauma as the people at the WTC in New York?

Taking in the crowd in front of the embassy. As usual, there's a terrible exhaust.

I eat lunch and go to the Nairobi Museum. It has a huge collection of birds. The anthropology room is also wonderful. While waiting in front of the Turkana Boy replica, Dr. Meave Leakey arrives. I listen to her explanation about Turkana Boy. Under what circumstances he died (in a flood), I'm surprised to hear in such detail how it was preserved, but of course it's all speculation.
After that, in Dr. Leakey's laboratory, we talk in front of the fossils. Her conclusion is that "education" is important to prevent the differences between us human beings, to stop us from going to a fight. Is that all? I'm wondering a little. According to Dr. Leakey, unlike Joyce Poole, who we talked about this later, we Homo Sapiens, like other apes, have limited aggression. According to her, the current aggression of humans is due to the stresses imposed by urbanization and population growth, and other species, if placed in narrow cages, will similarly become aggressive against that same species.
Here again, we must go to the apes to get an expert opinion on aggression. Would Jane Goodall provide that? (It's great to have three female researchers, Meave Leaky, Joyce Poole, and Jane Goodall!)[/i]

2002.02.06 Wednesday
@Nairobi[/b]

[i]I get up at 7:30. Departure is at 9. Taking in Nairobi National Park. From it you can see the city of Nairobi. When shooting in the grass, a tick climbed on my pants. At noon, we eat at the restaurant "Rangers" that is onsite. We drive overland to the Great Rift Valley. It takes about an hour and a half. We arrive at Joyce Poole's house on the edge of the rift area. All its energy comes from sunlight and wind. Water is pumped up from the river below. The rift side is covered with glass and the view is good, but it is extremely hot.
In Joyce's study I listen to her investigation into the elephant's vocal language. Great work. It's like making a dictionary of elephant languages. After that, I talk with Joyce in the living area. I ask heavy questions such as "Does humanity evolve ethically?" and "What can we do for the future?", but she answers sincerely.
According to Joyce, the aggression of us Homo Sapiens is genetically inherited from primates. Can't we go against the "selfish gene"? Can we evolve ethically with the intellectual powers we've been given? Joyce is not optimistic. This is because we have major problems with the environment, with politics, and economy. Will the environment last until that ethical evolution arrives.
Is a matrilineal society like that of the elephants key? "Is the birth of a female president the first step?" she jokes.[/i]

2002.02.07 Thursday
@Loiyangalani[/b]

[i]I wake up at 6:30. I separate out the luggage for Masai Mara and Lake Turkana. Departure is after 8. It's 2 hours from Wilson Airport in a large Cessna plane. We arrive at Lake Turkana. As soon as I get off, there is a tremendous amount of hot air. Strong winds like typhoons are blowing here all year round. We check in at the Oasis Club next to the runway. Inside the room it is 32.5 degrees. I'm off to eat lunch. This is the lodge where Peter Beard came almost every year and took pictures of naked women in the pool amid scenes of commotion. A German father was doing it too. The Turkana people around here became so upset by Peter that he was attacked and declared off limits, so he couldn't come anymore. (^^;

After lunch, I go to the shops outside the hotel, to buy sandals and shorts, and stop by the women's cultural center called "MOSARETU" in front of the hotel gate. This was set up to preserve something of the 4 tribes that live in this area, namely the El Molo, Samburu, Rendille, and Turkana folk art, crafts, music, and dance. The El Molo in particular are dwindling, only four unmixed persons are still alive. Apparently they mix with other tribes to prevent them from disappearing.
In the room, it's 36 degrees.

In the afternoon, I talk with Mr. Tsukimoto on the terrace while drinking a Kenyan beer called "Tusker". We discuss Afghanistan, 9/11, anthropology, apes, the Meiji Restoration, Hirobumi Ito, the great powers, the Pax Romana, imperialism, etc. until I can't speak anymore.
I get drunk by the third beer.

Japan had to reconsider before the Meiji Restoration. Perhaps it was the ultimate choice between being colonized or going over to the colonizing side.
Japan became a different country from the previous "Kuni". It was probably designed by Hirobumi Ito and others. Similar to what the great powers did, it was necessary to establish a constitutional monarchy, initiate an industrial revolution, and urgently arrange for setting up a national army. At the beginning of the Meiji government, the influence of the EU was large. Of course, at that time, the United States was a late-comer among the great empires. However, after the Sino-Japanese War and the Russo-Japanese War, Japan grew to a point where it turned the other great powers away from it. The same happened with Iraq 9 years ago. In the end, it was destroyed by a total attack of all the great powers.
For the great powers in the 19th century, Japan had a small land area and no resources, and like Hawaii and the Philippines, it was just one of the footholds for the Chinese market.
Afghanistan is in the midst of its Meiji Restoration. Fighting barbarism, but the opening up of the country has been a mixed affair and there is a dispute over the government.

Dinner. It's delicious. Bush pilot Alex, a joke-teller, has a serious side that consists of for many years counting and protecting the Amboseli elephants. He is an interesting man.
Even at night, it is 36 degrees in the room.[/i]

2002.02.08 Friday
@Loiyangalani[/b]

[i]I wake up at 6 o'clock, eat at 6:30, leave the lodge at 7, and we take off at 7:30. We're off to Nariokotome. Its meaning is "black elephant". Is there an elephant connection?
We land on the runway after a 50-minute flight. The wind is not so strong around here. Apparently the distance from here to the border of Ethiopia is 50km. We're also close to the Sudanese border. A car from a church preaching in this Turkana land is picking us up. One of the church preachers is Malaysian and the priest is Spanish.
After driving for about 15 minutes, we arrive at the place where Kamoya Kimeu found the bone of Turkana Boy. It is hot. I ask Kimeu to show me how to excavate, and I ask him to show me exactly where he found the bone. Mr. Kimeu is probably used to being interviewed a lot. My interview with Kimeu takes place in the hot sun.

For the last 40 years, he's been in contact with the Leaky family. He learned everything from Louis Leakey. When Richard became active, he worked with him for nearly a year. Homo erectus would have killed each other. Homo erectus may have been extinct by the time the next generation of larger-brained species arrived. However, he does not understand why humans cause such terrorism.

Aerial view with Alex in his Cessna.

We approach the Turkana youth who live here. Everyone can speak English thanks to the Christian mission. I am surprised when all of a sudden I'm asked, "Where do you think Osama bin Laden is?" Even in such a remote area, the information from the "empire" is transmitted sure enough. It's scary. However, those who know about the standard spin that's placed on it by the IMF and the WTO are not completely swallowing this "empire" propaganda. A reminder of "9/11" which I had forgotten about momentarily in such a remote place!

I return to Loiyangalani at 3 o'clock and have lunch. After the aerial shooting, Alex's Cessna got stuck in a runway dent and hurt its propeller. Alex is very depressed.
In the evening we go to an El Molo village. It's about 15 minutes by car from the lodge. It's a very beautiful place. If you forget the temperature, it looks like Scotland. The orange of the rocks illuminated by the setting sun, the blue-green of the lake, the yellow of the thin meadows, and the blue of the sky form a perfect contrast. We shoot film until sunset is complete.
8 o'clock, dinner. We have Nile perch every day, but I never tire of it. The chef here is very nice.
It's 38 degrees in the room at night. The electricity is switched off at 10 o'clock. I'm getting used to it a little, so I can sleep, but when a big wind blows, I wake up. So sleep is intermittent.[/i]

2002.02.09 Saturday
@Loiyangalani[/b]

[i]After a restless sleep, I wake up before 8 and have a meal. Mr. Kato[/i] (translator's note: refers to Naokuni Kato, a Kenya Professional Safari Guide) [i]also gets up. Then the bush pilots Alex and Eric. Maxi (4 years old), the child of the owner of the lodge, is cute. He may be a Lyall Watson in the future.
I talk to Alex. About the charm of Amboseli. About a study of the Amboseli ecosystem. The ambiguity of environmental guardians. He's a very interesting guy so I'd like to interview him someday.
(Alex's site: www.pixldesigns.com/maisha/)[/i] (translator's note: this link does not work anymore, but "Alex the bush pilot" probably refers to this person: Alexis Peltier)
[i]After the meal, we interview Mr. Kato for "Unfinished" magazine. Apparently, for Masai Mara's nature, it'd be better to stop sightseeing for about 10 years and leave it alone.
After 12 o'clock, the temperature in the room is 38 degrees. It seems my body has adapted, and I finally feel only a little sweaty at 35 degrees.
Lunch.
After 3:30, I go to the cape at the end of the El Molo village to shoot. A great view. I don't know where this is. A helicopter shoots over. Finally, Alex flies low as a "Greetings". After that, I take a picture in the village.

Dinner. I chat with Alex and others. Take a swim in the pool. Chat again by the pool. The lights go out and the stars appear to fall.
I go to bed at midnight. The temperature is 31 degrees. It feels a little cold. (^^;
At night, I wake up once due to a big blow of wind. I'm used to it now. When we go to Masai Mara, it may be too quiet and I'll be scared to sleep. (^^;[/i]

2002.02.10 Sunday
@Loiyangalani[/b]

[i]I get up at 7:30. Breakfast.

I'm reading "World History #27 - From the post Cold War period to the 21st Century".
I wonder if the cosmopolitanism that I used to idealize is nothing more than the American internationalism that spread around the west in the pseudo-peace of the Cold War.

Lunch at 12 o'clock.
We're shooting the dance from 4:30 on. The dance is great. Men hold hands, and men and women hold hands. The dance is like "Hana Ichi Monme". Openly erotic. Generations range from teens to grandfathers and grandmothers. Everyone is playing lively. I really enjoy the fun of their playing. The dynamics of the black skin on the muscles is wonderfully beautiful. I think it's more musical than the Masai. Masai music is still militant and solid. Men and women do not hold hands. I have seen many times that places in which the performing arts are well developed are peaceful places. Isn't this a universal aspect?

When I am about to go back after shooting at the lakeside, I meet a little boy carrying water and going home. Since it's such a small child that is out here walking with the heavy water, I approach him to put it in the car, and at that moment the boy is beautifully silhouetted in the sunset, but when I pull out the camera, the boy suddenly starts to cry with stones in both hands. According to the local staff, it seems the people around here believe the camera will pull out their soul. I did something poor. I deeply regret trying to take a picture without permission.

8 o'clock, dinner. Pool. Before 11, I'm off. It is pitch black. Room temperature, 32 degrees.[/i]

2002.02.11 Monday
@Loiyangalani
>>Masai Mara[/b]

[i]Temperature, 30 degrees (at its lowest this time). I get up around 6:30. Breakfast. I talk to Eric. He has been on a plane since he was 14 years old in France. He got his license at the age of 17 and after that went to Quebec, Canada for a while. However, he came to Africa because he didn't have a good job. He's very happy with the work here. When he flew to Sudan, he got involved in a civil war and was detained for a month.

We depart from the lodge at 9 o'clock and take off after 10. We land at Masai Mara at 12 o'clock and arrive at the lodge after 1. Just then Alex's Cessna happens to fly over.

After all this, Masai Mara is good. It's cool, green, and there are white clouds. The savanna is good. I enter the room. All rooms are the same, so the memories of the year before last and from last year can be revived.
8 o'clock, dinner. I chat at the bar. I send an email using Mr. Kato's computer. Go to bed before 12.[/i]

2002.02.12 Tuesday
@Masai Mara[/b]

[i]I wake up at 4:15. At 5 o'clock we depart for Governors Camp. We take in the sunrise in front of the balloon. We drive to the landing point of the balloon by car for some "aerial photography". The sunrise, a herd of elephants, and the balloon line up, so we shoot a "three-piece combination". It is great timing. However, one elephant is nervous and is about to get angry. The ranger we are with is also quite nervous. Two young male lions walk by. We stand in the savanna for the "aerial photography". There is light tension. Cheetahs may be lurking. Beside us a ranger stands guard with an automatic rifle.

We return to Mpata Lodge and have breakfast. Then I take a nap.
I get up at 12 o'clock. Lunch.
Departure for school at 2:30. We arrive in less than an hour. The children sing and welcome us. We set up the piano. Rehearsal. When I finish playing "Merry", it suddenly rains, so I joke that "Merry" is music for "rain-making" that brings blessings to Africa.
When I call the children over and ask, "What is this?", only one answers with "piano". Of course, it's the first time everyone sees and hears it. First touch by the children. This is a mistake. Now I play "Merry". The reaction is not very good. Next an improvisation. The reaction is good. Next is "Bolerish". The reaction is not good. However, "Bolerish" when played in African lands is surreal. The children sing and dance in return. It's amazing.

It was amazing to be absorbed in those children when they touched the piano. I think I've lost that curiosity and desire for expression. Even when I'm playing the piano, I can see that I'm sick because I'm wanting to touch a piano. Well, playing music is more fun than listening to it.

From the impressions of the children of "Merry", it was interesting they said "it's like a dance song" and "like an English song". Also, it was good that the girl who did so well when she led the singing said, "I knew what kind of song it was".

From the school to my favorite rock. We shoot until it gets dark. It's cold. However, this rock is the ultimate "healing". When you lie down on a rock, it's so comfortable that you don't want to leave.

After all that, we go back to Mpata. 8 o'clock, dinner. We drink Tio Pepe and white wine.
After 10 o'clock, I return to my room. I go to bed after 11.[/i]

2002.02.13 Wednesday
@Masai Mara[/b]

[i]I get up at 6 o'clock, have a shower and take a picture of the sunrise at 6:30. The song of the bird is amazing. I had a great dream, but I've forgotten it. My right shoulder hurts. I don't know why, it's a pain I've never experienced.

Breakfast at 7:30.
We depart for Nature Walk at 8:30. We go offroad and through the bushes. Some young Masai naturalists are our guide. People live in places like this. Unlike the Masai who live in the savanna, here corn is also cultivated. The children are excited because it's not often cars are coming here.
It should have been 1 hour but it took 2 hours to arrive.
We enter the forest. A "holy tree" grows here. Unlike in the savanna, the number of species here is overwhelmingly large, they form a complex ecosystem. Here plants coexist while trying out various defense measures, so you need to take many medicines. There are 3 types of medicine for malaria alone.

Unfortunately, we don't have much time, but if I were to come back I would not get tired of walking around this forest for half a day.

The planned talk between the Masai elders and youth has been postponed until tomorrow.

When we return to Mpata after another two hours, Joyce has already arrived. I talk with Joyce over lunch.
After 3 we depart to observe the elephants with Joyce.
It's difficult to get close to the herd of elephants, but eventually we manage enter the herd. I play music towards the elephants. The elephant that leads the herd likes "Merry". In response, a young elephant plays with grass, and a child elephant looks up strange. While doing this, we get caught up in a storm. A pitch black cloud. Huge lightning. The sun shines on the savanna in the foreground, in it is the herd of elephants. But the sky beyond is pitch black. What a landscape! It's past 6:30 when we leave the reserve. In the storm, we drive along the bumpy road and return to Mpata. Amid great rain and thunder.
8 o'clock, dinner. Lots of talking with Joyce. It's not enough, we continue talking at the bar. According to a study by the Guggenheim Foundation, "Aggression" is out there.
I return to my room at 11:30. I got a little drunk.[/i]

2002.02.14 Thursday
@Masai Mara[/b]

[i]I get up before 7 o'clock. It looks like I drank a little too much last night. My head is dumb.
Joyce and I have breakfast at 8. I hear the story of CD, the Amboseli research project.
At 9 we depart for a Masai village in Kichwa Tembo. I am supposed to talk to the village elders and a few young people, but it is canceled due to the morning rain, which is rare in Masai Mara. Is it the influence of El Niño? If this is an El Niño year, then Masai Mara will be flooded and it won't be possible to carry out game drives.

I'm visiting various parts of Mpata in the morning. The bar, the DEN library, etc.

◆ If the aggression of humankind comes from the "selfish gene", is there anything I can do about it?
◆ The time-scale of biological evolution is millions of years. However, our science and technology is developing year by year. It's too late to wait for biological evolution to stop the aggression.
◆ The Korean Peninsula and the Japanese were a 1000-year-old "family" but now a different, "divided family".
◆ Africans and the Japanese are "divided families" by millions of years.

After lunch, by 2 o'clock we go to the nearby village that is home to Ben and interview the Masai elders and youngsters. Surprisingly, the young people claim they saw the WTC incident on TV. They also seem to be aware of environmental destruction. When outsiders come to Masai Mara to live here, they say they will fight to get rid of them. Also, during the colonial era, if a person was killed, the elders properly searched for the criminal, but after the liberation, they stopped searching. So the colonial era was better. It's impressive they were lamenting the people that are now being killed like animals.

We shoot a scene in which I write an email in a tent in Kichwa Tembo. I get a last impression of the grasslands of Masai Mara where "Out of Africa" was shot. The savanna is darkening.

After 8 o'clock, we have a fun dinner. There is a Masai dance. There is the wedding ceremony of a Japanese couple. I'm tired. I'm going back to my room tonight without stopping at the bar.[/i]

2002.02.15 Friday
@Masai Mara to Nairobi[/b]

[i]I wake up at 7 o'clock. I was in the middle of some dream. i don't remember it. I get up from bed with the voice of a bird I'm hearing for the first time. I absent-mindedly start packing my luggage.
Breakfast.
More packing.
We depart Mpata at 10 o'clock. Along the way, Ben from the Masai village is waiting on the road and gives us a present. What a nice guy! Ben also gets in the car and we go straight to the runway.
At 11, we travel to Nairobi via Air Kenya. At two places along the way a stop is made to pick up more passengers. Full. Elderly American tourists.
We arrive in Nairobi after 12.
At 3, we have a meeting with Mr. Yoshikai and Mr. Tsukimoto.[/i]  (translator's note: Toshiya Yoshikai and Yutaka Tsukimoto, both involved in the composition and editing of this book)
[i]I call NY.
At 6:30, I leave the hotel and have dinner.
9 o'clock, airport. Take off is due at 11.[/i]

2002.2.16. Saturday
@Nairobi to London, N.Y.[/b]

[i]I arrive in London at 5am. After a 4 hour wait I head to New York. Arrival at JFK at 11:30 am. I get home by 1 o'clock. Start reading nearly 1000 emails. Go to a familiar restaurant for dinner. By chance I meet 42754. We promise to meet again.[/i]

[u]The transcript of the dialogue between Yoko Ono and Ryuichi Sakamoto translates as follows[/u]:

The Dance of Life

On the day he returned to NYC from Africa, Ryuichi Sakamoto happened to meet Yoko Ono.
They only exchanged greetings, but he realized the "elephantism" inside him made him want to collaborate with Yoko.
The following dialogue between the two took place at a later date.[/b]

Sakamoto: [i]Mankind hasn't had much history since it first appeared on earth. I think we're still in our childhood, as a kind of seed.[/i]
Ono: [i]I think we're still at the embryonic stage rather than childhood. I think these are embryonic (fetal) times. We haven't been born yet. By that time our heads are still asleep. After you are born and start toddling, your head will finally start working. You start to observe things around you and understand relationships with others. In the same way, the fact that humans are gradually able to go to other stars and communicate with other species may be because they've just been born. I think humans are still really young. I think they have great potential. So I think it's such a stupid thing to self-destruct as we're now doing. We have the wisdom to live, the motivation, and the power. For that reason, I think humans are still irreplaceable animals. Humans can make choices. You can choose what to eat to survive, meat or vegetables. I think it's amazing. Humans do not have animal or instinctive sex. It is not fixed. In that sense, we can be proud. Many young people these days hate humans and hate being a human. Maybe it's because they haven't yet realized their potential.[/i]
Sakamoto: [i]Wouldn't a generation like us have to clarify things and show them that 90 percent of their potential is still undiscovered?[/i]
Ono: [i]Recently there was a scientific experiment that I thought was amazing. Cells collected from a human mouth were transferred to a petri dish and taken to a separate room. Then, when the human subject was shown a violent image, the cells in the petri dish in the separate room showed a reaction. People say movies have no effect, but that's not the case. And the same reaction occurs even if you have the cells collected 50 miles away. Just by watching a film.
Not only do brain cells have memory, but all cells have it. And wisdom too. And they are communicating. Actually, it's a matter of course. It's the same with mice. When the ship sinks, not just 1 of them jumps off the ship, but all mice do. Some kind of communication is going on. Even birds fly away when there is a fire in the forest. Humans are very communicative, aren't they? But not at the level of the brain. There is communication at the cellular level. In that sense, we're really smart from the start, and a lot has already been prepared at the cellular level. However, we intentionally become insensitive to be able to live in harmony with the structure of society. We pretend not to know. We are incredibly precise creatures that cannot be compared to computers. We are living in denial of that, for now.[/i]
Sakamoto: [i]Perhaps the possibilities of such creatures and the structure of society are not well balanced out.[/i]
Ono: [i]Because humans can communicate using cells that much, it is not necessary to stand on the street corner and raise a flag to appeal against the war. It's easy to imagine, simply imagine it. The important thing then is not to pray to avoid dying when ill, but to think about the illness first.
You're not imagining yourself as being healthy, you imagine you're being ill. Therefore the illness will continue. Instead of imagining war, we have to imagine a place where everyone lives in peace and with bright faces. The imagery has to be the same as in Imagine. So let's imagine this together.[/i]
Sakamoto: [i]For the same reason, I don't fight back. The anti-war stance is the fight. I turn it into "No War".[/i]
Ono: [i]"No War" is fine, isn't it?[/i]
Sakamoto: [i]I won't fight. But naturally there are various opinions. Amazing.[/i]
Ono: [i]Just now I remember, there was the Byakkotai in Japan a long time ago. A person who survived from that era, an old man who was almost 100 years old, I heard him talking on the radio when I was still small. When he was looking from behind a tree, a samurai who was said to be a master was surrounded by enemies. He managed to escape by avoiding the fight and was saved in the end. How he managed this is that if you hold a sword at a certain angle, you will never be able to cut it. With that stance, he held out on the spot. In the end, his kimono came off. But his life was saved. The person who was a child at that time and who had observed this situation said, "It looked like a dance".
I think during our lives all of us are executing that kind of dance of survival. I'm doing so. It's not about criticizing people, or wars, or getting angry or fighting, it's just about dancing.[/i]
Sakamoto: [i]That is beautiful.[/i]

Interview arranged by 4286840 / Produce Center Co., Ltd.

The monthly Sotokoto magazine published this "Yoko Ono x Ryuichi Sakamoto" dialogue twice, in the June and July 2002 issues.

This compilation was released after an injunction was served against the band by MCA/Unicorn Records for breach of copyright. The ruling prohibited the band from releasing any music using the 'Black Flag' name or logo.
In an attempt to bypass the legal requirement, the band individually credited the performers on the front cover and censored the artwork. 
In spite of this, however, the logo is uncensored on the labels (however some copies allegedly had it manually censored with black marker) and the word "BLACK" in the title on the cover is written in the font usually used for the band's wordmark. Future (uncensored) pressings would use the same font as the other two words in the title.
1143204.title: Everything Went Black

Med "10-20-30" begår Per Vers den første bokssæt-udgivelse indenfor dansk rap! En trilogi af mixtapes der fejrer hhv. Pers 10 år som MC på fuld tid, 20 år med dansk rap på plade, og at det er præcis 30 år siden at den første rap-single "Rapper's Delight", udkom i USA. Der sælges 1000 eksklusive bokssæt KUN GENNEM RUN FOR COVER, og alt overskud går til Dansk Røde Kors og deres arbejde for at afhjælpe den ufattelige katastrofe på Haiti. Så hvis du kun køber en dansk rap-udgivelse i år, så lad det være denne. En født klassiker, undergrund i sit væsen, men super-luksuriøst præsenteret og pakket ind! 
INDHOLD:



STATUS

Indeholder 10 numre fra Per Vers' 10 forskellige mixtapes/selvudgivne CD'er gennem hans 10 år som professionel rapper. De fleste af disse numre har kun været udgivet på ultra-limited CD'er. Indeholder desuden 2 nye numre, samt fem interludes hvor Per går igennem sit bagkatalog sammen med the one and only Hans Otto Bisgaard, og hvor de to herrers replikker bliver cuttet op af DJ Static - mellemspil som man aldrig har set det før! 

15 tracks, 60 minutter.



DANISH OPERATION 

Er en hyldest til det gadelydbillede der fik en stor del af den danske hiphops mere erfarne folk igang, nemlig halvfemsernes beat-arkitekt, DJ Premier. Per V har inviteret sine homies til at "spytte over deres yndlings Premier beat". Den samlede deltagerliste lyder: JOE TRUE, JOKEREN. TEGNEDRENGEN, JOOKS, MIKKEL MUND, JONNY HEFTY, JØDEN, HENNING WINTHER, MAGERMAYN, TYDE T, ATAF KHAWAJA, STRØM, FANTOMET, PEDE B, MIKL, MC EINAR og JAZZY HAZ, samt mixes af DJ STATIC og DJ NOIZE - og selvfølgelig PER VERS, der leverer 4 numre.

30 tracks, 61 minutter.



RHYME TRAVELING 

Er en tidsrejse gennem hiphoppens historie. En "kronologisk collage". Den engelske DJ Jaguar Skills, der ugentligt bestyrer det mest hørte mixshow på BBC1, tager os fra "Rapper's Delight" i 1979 og frem til 2009 - "30 år på 60 minutter" - og over 500 klassiske skiver skæres i småstykker undervejs på bedste Guiness Rekordbog-manér! Hr. Vers blander sig vokalt med 30 små vers, eet pr. år, der på humoristisk maner oversætter eller kommenterer på de amerikanske hits. Tidsrejsen er blevet lagt på DVD, for at give plads til ekstramateriale i form af en 45 minutters claymation-animation incl. trackliste og en bid af verdens første "Mixtape Movie".

31 tracks, 62 minutter (+ 52 minutters ekstramateriale).

12317533.notes:
(Oregon)
Produced by Gene Breeden, this is the second excellent album released on the Ripcord-affiliated Verla Records label based in Albany, Oregon. The label was co-owned by an imprint which seems to have been co-owned by country singer Lonnie Coleman. He sings backup on this album, amid a studio crew populated by the Ripcord house band -- producer Gene Breeden on lead guitar and steel, his son Danny on drums, Gene Brown playing steel guitar, Gino Keyes on piano, Ellis Miller playing bass. Probably from McCoy's own group, the Real McCoys, are Randy McCoy on bass, David Dixon and Danny Turner playing guitar, and DeWayne Wear on fiddle. As the liner notes inform us, these guys were playing at a Eugene nightclub called the Embers Club, where they had been the house band for eight years before cutting this album. All the tracks on this album are original songs, most written by Billy McCoy, with one credited to Tide Cartwright, one to Lonnie Coleman, and one where Coleman and McCoy share the credits. No date is provided but the Library Of Congress lists several of these songs as having been registered in 1977, which may have also been the release date of the record. (slipcue.com)

12807194.notes:
"A Division of Premier Albums, Inc."

UTS 127 is on the labels which are yellow with black text.  On Side A, dead wax is stamped "Stereo #070759."  On Side B, "Audiomatrix" and "Bell Sound" are stamped on dead wax.

Notes from submission for UT 127:  "There is an interesting anomaly in this release.  The Matrix/Runouts of the discs apparently contain two matrix numbers: CS 81 and UTS-127.  The second number corresponds to the catalog number printed on the sleeve of this Celebrity release.  The first number, however, is the catalog number of an album released by Coronet Records that has the same track list as the Celebrity release.  In itself, there is nothing unusual about that.  Both Coronet and Celebrity are labels of Premier Albums, Inc. and both labels released many of the same albums, often using the same master stampers. What is unusual, however, is that the matrix number printed on the labels is reported to be UTS 127, not UT-127 as would be expected.   The designation “NEW” in the matrix number ordinarily indicates that an album that originally had been issued with a particular catalog number was being reissued with the same catalog number but with a “NEW” track list.   In this particular case, however, the track list on the UT (NEW)-127 labels, according to the initial submitter, is not a new track list.  It is the old track list found on the Coronet CX 81 and the Celebrity UT-127 releases.  If the information submitted is correct, then this would mean that a matrix number intended to be used with a new track list was used instead with an old track list.  That would be most unusual, to say the least. Unfortunately, the original submitter did not include images of the labels, so there is no way to determine what the facts of the matter really are."

Presented by veteran electronic soul label Tru Thoughts, and carefully curated by the imprint’s US label manager Jasmine De La Paz, Label Love Vol. 7 showcases 16 free tracks from nine labels around the world. With each label bringing a unique sonic signature and ethos, the compilation seamlessly unites genre-bending tunes, pulling together nostalgic classics, unreleased rarities and exclusive gems.

The series growing in stature with each edition, Vol. 7 presents music from Erased Tapes, Five Easy Pieces, Finders Keepers, Soundway Records, Strut Records, Tru Thoughts, World Circuit, ZZK Records, and !K7. This rare selection brings cuts from Sun Ra Quartet, Jane Weaver, Quantic Presents The Western Transient, Rival Consoles and Flako, to name a few, setting truly iconic artists side-by-side with the cream of current talent.

Via this mind-opening bundle of sounds – compiled simply for the love of sharing them with the universe – Label Love continues its mission to unite music creators and purveyors from around the world in spreading the gospel of good music to all."
13047270.title: Label Love Vol. 7

There are THREE distinct versions of this song, all sourced from the master.

Version 1: The original, undamaged, unedited master recording of Fats’ “Blueberry Hill,” was first pressed up on 78rpm. 

Version 2: The master tape, somehow, was damaged (stretched) for a moment and it created a ‘wow’ that can be heard at apx. 1:06 in the song during the lyric phrase “..vows we made.”   This is the version that appears on all 45rpms on the Red / Maroon labels and a few of the black labels as well. Different 45 pressing plants used the same master tape so it exists on several different versions of the record, including some foreign pressings.

Version 3: Somebody spotted the ‘wow’ and repaired it. They took the similar phrase from the end of the song, copied and edited it into the damaged portion of the master. However, in the original song he sings “…vows WE made..” in the early part, and “…vows YOU made..” (a lyrical mistake) in the later portion. That was the part that was up-spliced to fix the song, changing the lyric so it says “..vows YOU made..” in both spots. This is the version that is on most black label 45s, all LPs and CD versions and has become the master recording since 1957 into the digital age. 


Red label version; for maroon label version, see: 6868968.

New Orleans R&B

13576474.notes:
Imagen Latina is an album by Venezuelan musician Alberto Naranjo, originally released in 1992 and reedited twice in 2002 and 2008. It is the seventh album (fifth studio album) of El Trabuco Venezolano musical project arranged and directed by Naranjo.

Trabuco is a Spanish term used in Venezuelan baseball slang to describe an All-Star selection of players. So, El Trabuco Venezolano means "The Venezuelan All-Star Band", in the best sense of the phrase. Naranjo (b. Caracas, 1941 - d. Caracas, 2020) is one of Venezuela's icons of contemporary music, establishing his prestige as an arranger, conductor, composer and drummer. In 1992 Naranjo produced Imagen Latina. Soloists with an already established career in Venezuela participated in this project; renowned salseros as Canelita Medina, Carlos Espósito, Vladimir Lozano, Trina Medina, Carlos Daniel Palacios and Mauricio Silva; noted folklorists as Simón Díaz, Cecilia Todd and the group Serenata Guayanesa, and also counted with the collaboration of poet Jesús Rosas Marcano, musician Benjamín Brea, pop singer María Rivas, jazz pianist Otmaro Ruiz, and the polifacetic Aldemaro Romero. Most salsa bands are a tightly wound unit that developed their music through years of playing in clubs around their hometown. El Trabuco Venezolano never subscribed to that aesthetic. As the vehicle for the arrangements of Naranjo, his Trabuco defied all salsa conventions in the 1970s. The eclectic body of Naranjo's work shows some debt to Billo Frómeta, Tito Puente and the Thad Jones/Mel Lewis Big Band, preferring traditional guaracha, jazz, bolero, mambo and Venezuelan genres, creating a sophisticated and distinctive sound with accessible melodic hooks, complex harmonies and time signatures, as well as a special devotion to the recording studio. This record was never released outside of Venezuela, and after ten years of relative obscurity, the company Merusa Records of Netherlands introduced it at the international level.

13979237.notes:
Imagen Latina is an album by Venezuelan musician Alberto Naranjo, originally released in 1992 and reedited twice in 2002 and 2008. It is the seventh album (fifth studio album) of El Trabuco Venezolano musical project arranged and directed by Naranjo.

Trabuco is a Spanish term used in Venezuelan baseball slang to describe an All-Star selection of players. So, El Trabuco Venezolano means "The Venezuelan All-Star Band", in the best sense of the phrase. Naranjo (b. Caracas, 1941 - d. Caracas, 2020) is one of Venezuela's icons of contemporary music, establishing his prestige as an arranger, conductor, composer and drummer. In 1992 Naranjo produced Imagen Latina. Soloists with an already established career in Venezuela participated in this project; renowned salseros as Canelita Medina, Carlos Espósito, Vladimir Lozano, Trina Medina, Carlos Daniel Palacios and Mauricio Silva; noted folklorists as Simón Díaz, Cecilia Todd and the group Serenata Guayanesa, and also counted with the collaboration of poet Jesús Rosas Marcano, musician Benjamín Brea, pop singer María Rivas, jazz pianist Otmaro Ruiz, and the polifacetic Aldemaro Romero. Most salsa bands are a tightly wound unit that developed their music through years of playing in clubs around their hometown. El Trabuco Venezolano never subscribed to that aesthetic. As the vehicle for the arrangements of Naranjo, his Trabuco defied all salsa conventions in the 1970s. The eclectic body of Naranjo's work shows some debt to Billo Frómeta, Tito Puente and the Thad Jones/Mel Lewis Big Band, preferring traditional guaracha, jazz, bolero, mambo and Venezuelan genres, creating a sophisticated and distinctive sound with accessible melodic hooks, complex harmonies and time signatures, as well as a special devotion to the recording studio. This record was never released outside of Venezuela, and after ten years of relative obscurity, the company Merusa Records of Netherlands introduced it at the international level.

14195988.notes:
10-CD boxed set (LP-format) with 224 page hardcover book, 299 tracks. Total playing time approx. 738 minutes.
The compelling story of how a country music cottage industry transformed Bakersfield into the Country Music Capital of the West, sometimes called ‘Nashville West’, a serious challenge to Nashville's commercial country dominance.
This first sprawling multi-disc anthology begins with 1940s field recordings of migrants, all the way through 1974, with profiles on each artist.
Including a larger number of previously unreleased studio and live recordings, radio recordings and demos.
A treasure trove of Bakersfield history presenting country music stars Merle Haggard and Buck Owens, guitar hero Don Rich and dozens of artists like Ferlin Husky, Dallas Frazier, Jean Shepard, Wynn Stewart, Tommy Duncan, Red Simpson, Kay Adams, Duck Curless, Joe Maphis, David Frizzell, The Gosdin Brothers, Clarence White a.m.o.
From hits to deep cuts to alternate takes to album tracks to live material, this set dives deeper into the Bakersfield Sound than ever before.Full-color illustrated 224-page hardcover book with a plethora of photos, many shown here for the first time, and track-by-track commentary .
In depth analysis by Grammy-nominated Bakersfield Sound historian Scott B. Bomar.
Foreword by Foo Fighters guitarist Chris Shiflett.

Due to a legal claim just prior to the release date, eight songs have been removed from the CDs (replaced by a brief silence). These songs are still listed in the book. Copies also seem to exist on which these songs are present. The removed songs are 5-6, 5-7, 10-7, 10-8, 10-9, 10-10, 10-11, 10-26.

Singers: Rev. Jerry Williams, Dolores Gibbons, Minnie Williams,  Wilbert Richardson, Johnny Hickman

Instrumental: Piano, Michael Mazyck; Organ, Garry Jones
_____
Not listed in the liner notes, but album was produced by members and a minister of Trinity United Methodist Church, 375 Broad St, Providence, RI. The Providence Journal lists a Rev. Jerry Williams as being hired on there as a "director of neighborhood ministries" in November 1971 (November 20, 1971 article). The singing group was formed June 1971, and Jerry Williams left the group after their last anniversary concert on June 29, 1974, indicated from another Journal article printed that day.

According to the same article Rev. Williams, prior to serving as outreach minister in Rhode Island, previously toured the US from 1955-1970 as a backup singer with a number of gospel acts, including Mahalia Jackson, Mighty Clouds of Joy, and the Swanee Quintet. Also noted to have served as a columnist for "Gospel Rama" in Tennessee. Group was noted to have given benefit concerts at other churches, homeless shelters, prisons, etc. Rev. Williams gave his reason for ending his leadership of the group as needing to dedicate more of his time to church outreach.

14747245.notes:
Each week, ten musicians arrive at a former South Philadelphia funeral home where, one by one, they unload their old tube amps and vintage gear. Once inside, the classic sounds of the 1960s are reinvigorated, reenergized and reborn. Legends, like Stevie, Aretha and the Four Tops; lesser-known artists including Donny Hathaway, Arthur Conley and Betty Everett – all are given new life.

In a few short years the York Street Hustle has gone from filling tiny South Street bars to repeated sell outs of WXPN’s World Cafe Live. Their repertoire now spans over 80 songs including more than a decade worth of Detroit, Memphis and Chicago soul. This is not your typical Motown wedding band. With grit, sweat, and attention to detail, The York Street Hustle is the Northeast’s premier 10-piece 1960s soul tribute.

Notes for the bonus download tracks 19-33:

19 Dennis the Menace Go-Go Wah-Wah (1980) Unrelenting rocker off their rare EP.
20 The Dents Fear in the Western World (live on WAIF 1979) Tough Ultravox! cover comin' at ya. Cincy punk's great lost band?
21 The Customs She'll Always Be Mine (1980 rehearsal) Unearthed version of this Customs classic.
22 The Verbs Bouncin' the Beat (live 1979) Twistin' live at Wyoming High School. Let's bounce it!
23 The Dents Queen City Radio (live on WAIF 1979) Clash gem gets a Queen City makeover (sorry it cuts off). Up yours, 'EBN!
24 Dream 286 End of the World (1982) Icy postpunk coolness incarnate. Where were you in '82?
25 The Ed Davis Band Fuck Each Other(rehearsal 1977) Here's rough decadence for ya. "High on Sopors...this romance begins."
26 The Rave-N's Doomsday (studio recording 1979) Apocalyptic cut from these Northern Kentucky bruisers' unreleased 45.
27 The Customs Bring My Cadillac Back (1979 demo) Rare demo of the B side of the band's first single.
28 Alterior Motives Out of Touch (live 1981) Blown-out but undeniably powerful recording by Viv Pinger's post-Dents unit.
29 Latex Theatre Routine Pleasures (1981 demo) Another dark entry via one of Doug Halleť's fine outfits. Dig that synth solo.
30 The Spaztiks Ain't Nothin' to Do (1980 rehearsal) Dead Boys cover by guitarist William G. Weber's (Chrome Cranks, G.G. Allin) first band.
31 The Verbs Baby, Can I Walk You Home (live 1979) Punkified Brill Building/girl group pop mined from the Verbs' '79 high school date.
32 The Malcontent The Cockroach Creep (live 1979) Kafka meets Quicksilver(!) in this psych-punk nugget taped at Bogart's.
33 Ed Davis Band Keith Richards' Dead (1978) Cincinnati punk's official opening salvo. "No, no, not Keith Richards!"

Limited run of 200 copies released directly to record stores. Program repeats on both sides of record.
Info card includes states 'Thank you for running a record shop. Enclosed is a new EP & it is a strange bird. The album has a different tonality & therefore resonates in that manner. Hope you enjoy it over time. Recorded, mixed, & mastered specifically for Headphones Listening.'

The tracks on the album were recorded live to tape in many different locations - none of them were studios. This was done to achieve a "raw", live/ ambient recording tonality or soundscape. So instead of miking up the instruments/amps - the recording spaces themselves were miked in specific spots - the songs were then recorded as they were played live.
What you hear on the album is a direct representation of what was performed in real time.

17344597.notes:
CD edition with bonus DVD consisting of Modern Harmonic edit of the film plus bonus trailers and oddities.
8 panel cardboard package with OBI strip
Total duration 66:46
Tracks 7 to 10 =  CD only bonus tracks.

From out of a rotted tomb crawls the full score for the “film” Dracula (The Dirty Old Man)! Uncovered by archivist George Gimarc, these tapes, untouched for nearly 50 years and mislabelled "Sex Monsters," are finally dusted off, and you’ve never heard the music sound this good–the sound that made it into the film is an utter stake through the heart. Rumor has it that the audio from the original cut was so bad that they went back and redubbed everything (à la Woody Allen’s What’s Up, Tiger Lily?) to comedic effect. Who knew that buried under all that jabberwocky was a funk leaning jazz soundtrack that really grooves? This album comprises the highlights of the film score accompanied by audio cues believed to be Whit Boyd instructing the musicians in what was likely a live performance while watching the film.
17344597.title: Dracula (The Dirty Old Man) Original Motion Picture Soundtrack

20781862.notes: Frank y sus Inquietos is a little-commented Venezuelan treasure in our time, an amazing, almost unknown jewel of Venezuelan hard salsa, treasured with zeal by music lovers of all times. This group is evidence of the musical communion of the young Caracas of the late sixties with the sounds of the Caribbean in their nascent marriage with urban aggressiveness. As a result of these meetings of “friends who played instruments” such as congas, bongos, piano, timbales and their fiery discharges on the top floor of Block 3 of La Silsa, a building located in this humble and highly populated Caracas popular area, the repertoire of songs by the homonym Frank y sus Inquietos (1969), with an exquisite imagination and brimming with vitality, authentic vocals and choirs, overwhelming percussion, strong bass and fierce piano conducted by Frank González.
